claim: Faithful chromosome segregation in all eukaryotes relies on centromeres.
source: Faithful chromosome segregation in all eukaryotes relies on centromeres, the chromosomal sites that recruit kinetochore proteins and mediate spindle attachment during cell division.
evidence: This is a general statement about centromere function supported by established scientific knowledge and cited literature in the introduction.

claim: CenH3 is the defining chromatin component of centromeres in most eukaryotes, including animals, fungi, plants, and protists.
source: The centromeric histone H3 variant, CenH3, is the defining chromatin component of centromeres in most eukaryotes, including animals, fungi, plants, and protists.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific consensus and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: CenH3 was lost independently in at least four lineages of insects.
source: In this study, using detailed genomic and transcriptome analyses, we show that CenH3 was lost independently in at least four lineages of insects.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic and transcriptome data presented in the manuscript, including homology searches and phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Each of the four lineages that lost CenH3 represents an independent transition from monocentricity to holocentricity.
source: Each of these lineages represents an independent transition from monocentricity (centromeric determinants localized to a single chromosomal region) to holocentricity (centromeric determinants extended over the entire chromosomal length) as ancient as 300 million years ago.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses and cytological evidence from the literature.

claim: The transitions to holocentricity in insects occurred as ancient as 300 million years ago.
source: Each of these lineages represents an independent transition from monocentricity (centromeric determinants localized to a single chromosomal region) to holocentricity (centromeric determinants extended over the entire chromosomal length) as ancient as 300 million years ago.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic dating and cited literature on insect evolution.

claim: Holocentric insects contain a CenH3-independent centromere.
source: Holocentric insects therefore contain a CenH3-independent centromere, different from almost all the other eukaryotes.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of CenH3 in holocentric insects combined with the presence of other kinetochore components.

claim: Ancient transitions to holocentricity in insects obviated the need to maintain CenH3.
source: We propose that ancient transitions to holocentricity in insects obviated the need to maintain CenH3, which is otherwise essential in most eukaryotes, including other holocentrics.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the correlation between holocentricity and CenH3 loss.

claim: Kinetochore assembly onto centromeres occurs in a hierarchical process that strictly depends on the presence of CenH3 in animals, fungi, and plants.
source: In animals, fungi, and plants, kinetochore assembly onto centromeres occurs in a hierarchical process that strictly depends on the presence of the specialized histone H3 variant CenH3 (first identified as Cenp-A in mammals [Earnshaw and Rothfield, 1985; Palmer et al., 1991]), which replaces the canonical H3 in centromeric nucleosomes (Sullivan et al., 1994; Yoda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: CenH3 deletions are lethal and lead to catastrophic defects in chromosome segregation in all organisms that have been studied.
source: In all organisms that have been studied, CenH3 deletions are lethal and lead to catastrophic defects in chromosome segregation (Stoler et al., 1995; Buchwitz et al., 1999; Howman et al., 2000; Blower and Karpen, 2001; Talbert et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The presence of CenH3 defines both canonical centromeres and neocentromeres in diverse organisms.
source: Moreover, the presence of CenH3 defines both canonical centromeres and neocentromeres in diverse organisms (Dawson et al., 2007; Malik and Henikoff, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The presence of CenH3 homologs in all animals, fungi, and plants studied so far, together with their identification in distantly branching protist lineages has established the paradigm that CenH3-containing chromatin is an absolute requirement for centromere function.
source: The presence of CenH3 homologs in all animals, fungi, and plants studied so far, together with their identification in distantly branching protist lineages has established the paradigm that CenH3-containing chromatin is an absolute requirement for centromere function (Malik and Henikoff, 2003; Panchenko and Black, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents the prevailing scientific paradigm before this study.

claim: Multiple insect lineages have independently lost CenH3 despite preserving some other canonical kinetochore components.
source: In contrast to this prevailing paradigm, we show that multiple insect lineages have independently lost CenH3 despite preserving some other canonical kinetochore components.
evidence: This is supported by genomic and transcriptome data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CenH3 losses coincide with dramatic changes in centromere architecture.
source: These CenH3 losses coincide with dramatic changes in centromere architecture, suggesting that alternate centromere configurations may render the CenH3 protein dispensable.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between holocentricity and CenH3 loss.

claim: Alternate centromere configurations may render the CenH3 protein dispensable.
source: These CenH3 losses coincide with dramatic changes in centromere architecture, suggesting that alternate centromere configurations may render the CenH3 protein dispensable.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Monocentromeres can range dramatically in size, from 125 bp in budding yeasts to megabases in humans.
source: Monocentromeres can range dramatically in size, from 125 bp in budding yeasts to megabases in humans, and can be either genetically (sequence-dependent) or epigenetically defined.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Holocentromeres have kinetochores attached along the extensive segments or even the entire length of chromosomes.
source: In contrast, holocentromeres have kinetochores attached along the extensive segments or even the entire length of chromosomes.
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Holocentromeres were first described by Schrader in 1935.
source: First described by Schrader (1935), holocentromeres have been best studied in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (Dernburg, 2001; Maddox et al., 2004; Gassmann et al., 2012; Steiner and Henikoff, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to historical literature.

claim: Holocentricity appears to have evolved independently in multiple eukaryotic lineages by convergent evolution.
source: However, holocentricity appears to have evolved independently in multiple eukaryotic lineages by convergent evolution (Melters et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Holocentricity is believed to have evolved at least four times from monocentric ancestors in insects.
source: To gain insight into kinetochore changes associated with transitions to holocentricity, we focused on insects in which holocentricity is believed to have evolved at least four times from monocentric ancestors (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Whiting, 2002; Grimaldi and Engel, 2005; Savard et al., 2006) (modified from Melters et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CenH3 homologs were identified in the monocentric insect orders: Diptera (flies and mosquitoes), Hymenoptera (wasps, bees, and ants), and Coleoptera (beetles).
source: In addition to the well-studied CenH3 homologs in Drosophila species (Henikoff et al., 2000), we were able to identify CenH3 homologs in the monocentric insect orders: Diptera (flies and mosquitoes), Hymenoptera (wasps, bees, and ants), and Coleoptera (beetles) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by homology searches and data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CenH3 homologs were not found in any of the five sequenced holocentric lepidopteran species (butterflies and moths).
source: In contrast, we were unable to find CenH3 homologs in any of the five sequenced holocentric lepidopteran species (butterflies and moths) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by homology searches and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CenH3 was not found in two additional insect orders previously reported to be holocentric: Hemiptera (true bugs) and Phthiraptera (lice).
source: Extending our survey, we were similarly unable to find CenH3 in two additional insect orders previously reported to be holocentric: Hemiptera (true bugs) and Phthiraptera (lice).
evidence: This is supported by homology searches in genomic data.

claim: Hemiptera and Phthiraptera represent an independent transition to holocentricity in insects.
source: Together, these two orders represent an independent transition to holocentricity in insects (Figure 1A, 'Materials and methods') (Whiting, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses and citations.

claim: An additional H3-like gene found in the hemipteran pea aphid Acyrthosiphon pisum phylogenetically clustered with canonical H3 proteins, rather than CenH3s.
source: Although we found an additional H3-like gene in the hemipteran pea aphid Acyrthosiphon pisum, we found that it unambiguously phylogenetically clustered with canonical H3 proteins, rather than CenH3s (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,C).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: CenH3 is missing from all sequenced genomes from eight holocentric insect species.
source: Thus, CenH3 is missing from all sequenced genomes from eight holocentric insect species, but present in all sequenced monocentric insects.
evidence: This is supported by comprehensive homology searches in genomic data.

claim: CenH3 is present in all sequenced monocentric insects.
source: Thus, CenH3 is missing from all sequenced genomes from eight holocentric insect species, but present in all sequenced monocentric insects.
evidence: This is supported by homology searches in genomic data.

claim: Putative CenH3 homologs were identified in the assemblies of all monocentric insects from transcriptome analyses.
source: We were able to identify putative CenH3 homologs in the assemblies of all monocentric insects (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome assembly and homology searches.

claim: CenH3 could not be detected in the assemblies derived from any of the holocentric insects from transcriptome analyses.
source: In contrast to the monocentric insects, we could not detect CenH3 in the assemblies derived from any of the holocentric insects.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome assembly and homology searches.

claim: An H3-like gene obtained in the L. vibrans assembly phylogenetically groups with H3 rather than CenH3.
source: Although we did obtain an H3-like gene in the L. vibrans assembly, evolutionary analyses support its phylogenetic grouping with H3 rather than CenH3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Comparable or even higher number of predicted proteins were found in the holocentric compared to the monocentric assemblies.
source: Indeed, our analyses revealed comparable or even higher number of predicted proteins in the holocentric compared to the monocentric assemblies, implying at least equivalent transcriptome coverages of the holocentric and monocentric assemblies.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analyses of transcriptome assemblies using T. castaneum proteome as benchmark.

claim: CenH3 transcript abundance was at least at the 50th percentile in all monocentric insect assemblies except the cockroach assembly.
source: Second, we found that CenH3 transcripts are not rare in monocentric insects; CenH3 transcript abundance was at least at the 50th percentile in all instances except the cockroach assembly (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by transcript abundance analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: CenH3 is likely absent in the four holocentric odonatan and dermapteran insects examined.
source: We therefore conclude that CenH3 is likely absent in the four holocentric odonatan and dermapteran insects examined as it is absent in the genome sequences of the holocentric lepidopteran and hemipteran/phthirapteran insects.
evidence: This is inferred from transcriptome coverage and abundance analyses.

claim: Each of the four independent transitions to holocentricity in insects was associated with CenH3 loss.
source: Thus, we conclude that each of the four independent transitions to holocentricity in insects was associated with CenH3 loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between holocentricity and absence of CenH3 across multiple insect lineages.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses of CenH3 reveal a topology of insect CenH3s that is largely consistent with the expected branching order of the insect species.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of CenH3 and other H3 proteins based on their homologous histone-fold domains reveal a topology of insect CenH3s that is largely consistent with the expected branching order of the insect species (Whiting, 2002; Grimaldi and Engel, 2005; Savard et al., 2006) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), confirming that the absence of CenH3 in holocentric insects is due to recurrent loss rather than reinvention or horizontal transfer of CenH3 in monocentric insect lineages.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The absence of CenH3 in holocentric insects is due to recurrent loss rather than reinvention or horizontal transfer of CenH3 in monocentric insect lineages.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of CenH3 and other H3 proteins based on their homologous histone-fold domains reveal a topology of insect CenH3s that is largely consistent with the expected branching order of the insect species (Whiting, 2002; Grimaldi and Engel, 2005; Savard et al., 2006) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), confirming that the absence of CenH3 in holocentric insects is due to recurrent loss rather than reinvention or horizontal transfer of CenH3 in monocentric insect lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analyses.

claim: CenH3 was confirmed to be present in all (monocentric) coleopteran species from additional transcriptome assemblies.
source: These additional assemblies confirmed not only CenH3 presence in all (monocentric) coleopteran species (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), but also confirmed its absence in all hemipteran and lepidopteran species.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome assembly and homology searches.

claim: CenH3 is absent in all hemipteran and lepidopteran species from additional transcriptome assemblies.
source: These additional assemblies confirmed not only CenH3 presence in all (monocentric) coleopteran species (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), but also confirmed its absence in all hemipteran and lepidopteran species.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome assembly and homology searches.

claim: CenH3-like sequences obtained in two lepidopteran assemblies were unambiguously attributed to microsporidian contaminants via phylogenetic analyses.
source: Although we obtained CenH3-like sequences in two lepidopteran assemblies, we could unambiguously attribute them to microsporidian contaminants via phylogenetic analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: CenH3 loss probably preceded or occurred close to the emergence of lepidopteran and hemipteran/phthirapteran orders.
source: As a result, we estimate that CenH3 loss probably preceded or occurred close to the emergence of these insect orders, at least 120 million years ago in Lepidoptera (Hedges et al., 2006) and likely 300 million years ago in the common ancestor of Hemiptera and Phthiraptera (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of CenH3 in all species examined within these orders and phylogenetic dating.

claim: CenH3 loss occurred at least 120 million years ago in Lepidoptera.
source: As a result, we estimate that CenH3 loss probably preceded or occurred close to the emergence of these insect orders, at least 120 million years ago in Lepidoptera (Hedges et al., 2006) and likely 300 million years ago in the common ancestor of Hemiptera and Phthiraptera (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic dating from cited literature.

claim: CenH3 loss occurred likely 300 million years ago in the common ancestor of Hemiptera and Phthiraptera.
source: As a result, we estimate that CenH3 loss probably preceded or occurred close to the emergence of these insect orders, at least 120 million years ago in Lepidoptera (Hedges et al., 2006) and likely 300 million years ago in the common ancestor of Hemiptera and Phthiraptera (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic dating from cited literature.

claim: CenpI, CenpL/M/N, and the DNA-proximal CenpS/X proteins were identified in insect genomes and transcriptomes.
source: We identified CenpI, CenpL/M/N, and the DNA-proximal CenpS/X proteins.
evidence: This is supported by homology searches in genomic and transcriptomic data.

claim: The CenpS/X complex likely serves roles in DNA damage rather than at the kinetochore in insects since the CenpT/W proteins are absent.
source: We note that since the CenpT/W proteins, which are obligatory for the CenpS/X kinetochore function, are absent in all insects, it is likely that the CenpS/X complex serves roles in DNA damage (Singh et al., 2010) rather than at the kinetochore.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of CenpT/W proteins and cited literature on CenpS/X function.

claim: Several inner kinetochore components continue to be present even in the CenH3-deficient species.
source: Nonetheless, several inner kinetochore components continue to be present even in the CenH3-deficient species (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by homology searches and data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The recruitment of inner kinetochore components has been shown to depend on CenH3 in animals and fungi.
source: This is somewhat unexpected since the recruitment of these components has been shown to depend on CenH3 in animals and fungi (Westhorpe and Straight, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Holocentric insects may have adopted a CenH3-independent inner kinetochore assembly pathway.
source: It will therefore be important in future to test if these kinetochore components localize to centromeres in the absence of CenH3; this would imply that holocentric insects have adopted a CenH3-independent inner kinetochore assembly pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the presence of inner kinetochore components in CenH3-deficient species.

claim: CenpC was found to be absent from all insects that lack CenH3.
source: We did find the inner kinetochore protein CenpC to be absent from all insects that lack CenH3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by homology searches and data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CenpC is the direct DNA-binding partner of CenH3.
source: CenpC is the direct DNA-binding partner of CenH3 and together with CenH3 constitutes the centromere core components (Carroll et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The CenpC motif is universally found in CenpC proteins and has been shown to interact with the CenH3 C-terminus.
source: Of these, the CenpC motif is universally found in CenpC proteins and has been shown to interact with the CenH3 C-terminus (Kato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Most animal and fungal CenpC proteins contain a cupin fold domain about 100 amino acids downstream of the CenpC motif.
source: In addition, most animal and fungal CenpC proteins contain a cupin fold domain (Pfam PF00190), about 100 amino acids downstream of the CenpC motif (Talbert et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CenpC proteins from mayflies and stick insects (both monocentrics) possess both the CenpC motif and the associated cupin domain.
source: We found that CenpC proteins from mayflies and stick insects (both monocentrics) possess both the CenpC motif and the associated cupin domain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by homology searches and structural analyses shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Putative CenpC proteins from Hymenoptera and cockroach (also monocentric) contained the CenpC motif but not the cupin domain.
source: In contrast, putative CenpC proteins from Hymenoptera and cockroach (also monocentric) contained the CenpC motif but not the cupin domain.
evidence: This is supported by homology searches and structural analyses.

claim: The CenpC motif was not found in any of the holocentric species (genomes or transcriptomes).
source: We were unable to find the CenpC motif in any of the holocentric species (genomes or transcriptomes).
evidence: This is supported by homology searches.

claim: Holocentric dragonflies encode a protein with a clearly identifiable CenpC cupin domain but its CenpC motif has decayed.
source: Intriguingly, although holocentric dragonflies encode a protein with a clearly identifiable CenpC cupin domain (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), its CenpC motif has decayed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by homology searches and phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: CenH3 loss in dragonflies may have allowed the degeneration of its CenpC motif since the CenpC motif interacts with CenH3.
source: We speculate that since the CenpC motif interacts with CenH3, CenH3 loss in dragonflies may have allowed the degeneration of its CenpC motif.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the known interaction between CenpC motif and CenH3.

claim: The absence of CenH3-interacting CenpC motifs in dragonflies and other holocentric insects serves as an independent confirmation for the losses of CenH3 in these lineages.
source: The absence of CenH3-interacting CenpC motifs in dragonflies and other holocentric insects also serves as an independent confirmation for the losses of CenH3 in these lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between CenH3 loss and CenpC motif decay.

claim: Homologs of outer kinetochore components including Ndc80 and Mis12 are almost universally conserved in most insect orders.
source: In contrast to the variation in inner kinetochore protein repertoires, homologs of outer kinetochore components including Ndc80 and Mis12 are almost universally conserved in most insect orders (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by homology searches and data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Insects vary widely in the DNA-proximal part of their kinetochore but have largely conserved the means to attach the kinetochore to the spindle apparatus.
source: This suggests that although insects vary widely in the DNA-proximal part of their kinetochore, they have largely conserved the means to attach the kinetochore to the spindle apparatus.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of outer kinetochore components despite variation in inner components.

claim: Holocentric insects likely employ CenH3-independent ways of connecting centromeric DNA to the rest of a relatively conserved kinetochore complex.
source: This further implies that holocentric insects likely employ CenH3-independent ways of connecting centromeric DNA to the rest of a relatively conserved kinetochore complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of CenH3 but presence of outer kinetochore components.

claim: Findings in holocentric insects contrast with the recent findings of CenH3 absence in kinetoplastids, which not only lack CenH3 but also possess an entirely different repertoire of kinetochore proteins.
source: Our findings in holocentric insects contrast with the recent findings of CenH3 absence in kinetoplastids, which not only lack CenH3 but also possess an entirely different repertoire of kinetochore proteins (Akiyoshi and Gull, 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature on kinetoplastids.

claim: Findings in holocentric insects are reminiscent of male meiosis in holocentric C. elegans, in which the outer kinetochore components appear to localize independent of CenH3.
source: Our findings are more reminiscent of male meiosis in holocentric C. elegans, in which the outer kinetochore components appear to localize independent of CenH3 (Monen et al., 2005); CenH3 is nevertheless essential for C. elegans mitosis (Buchwitz et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature on C. elegans.

claim: CenH3 is essential for C. elegans mitosis.
source: Our findings are more reminiscent of male meiosis in holocentric C. elegans, in which the outer kinetochore components appear to localize independent of CenH3 (Monen et al., 2005); CenH3 is nevertheless essential for C. elegans mitosis (Buchwitz et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Holocentric insects account for 16% of all named eukaryotic species.
source: Thus, holocentric insects, which account for 16% of all named eukaryotic species (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005), appear to be unique among complex eukaryotes in entirely losing their dependence on CenH3s.
evidence: This is based on a citation to literature on species diversity.

claim: Holocentric insects appear to be unique among complex eukaryotes in entirely losing their dependence on CenH3s.
source: Thus, holocentric insects, which account for 16% of all named eukaryotic species (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005), appear to be unique among complex eukaryotes in entirely losing their dependence on CenH3s.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing CenH3 loss in holocentric insects but not in other eukaryotes.

claim: Independent transitions to holocentricity preceded the losses of CenH3s in insects.
source: Given the essential requirement of CenH3 for chromosome segregation in monocentric contexts as shown in Drosophila melanogaster (Blower and Karpen, 2001), we hypothesize that independent transitions to holocentricity preceded the losses of CenH3s in insects.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the essential role of CenH3 in monocentric organisms.

claim: Other holocentric animals (including other arthropods) and plants still encode for CenH3.
source: However, since other holocentric animals (including other arthropods) and plants still encode for CenH3 (Buchwitz et al., 1999; Heckmann et al., 2011) (Figure 2—source data 1), we speculate that another, distinct event allowing CenH3 loss in holocentric insects must have occurred early in insect evolution, in the common ancestor of dragonflies and flies (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Another, distinct event allowing CenH3 loss in holocentric insects must have occurred early in insect evolution, in the common ancestor of dragonflies and flies.
source: However, since other holocentric animals (including other arthropods) and plants still encode for CenH3 (Buchwitz et al., 1999; Heckmann et al., 2011) (Figure 2—source data 1), we speculate that another, distinct event allowing CenH3 loss in holocentric insects must have occurred early in insect evolution, in the common ancestor of dragonflies and flies (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the phylogenetic distribution of CenH3 loss.

claim: The lineage-specific evolutionary invention of a centromeric protein may have conferred independently derived holocentric lineages with a unique ability to carry out mitosis in a CenH3-independent manner.
source: Such a determinant may have been the lineage-specific evolutionary invention of a centromeric protein (Ross et al., 2013), which may have conferred these independently derived holocentric lineages with a unique ability to carry out mitosis in a CenH3-independent manner, thereby relaxing the selective pressure to maintain CenH3 in the genome.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the pattern of CenH3 loss.

claim: Changes in centromere architecture may have rendered dispensable one of the most defining proteins associated with centromere function in almost all eukaryotes.
source: Thus, changes in centromere architecture may have rendered dispensable one of the most defining proteins associated with centromere function in almost all eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a concluding interpretation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Bombyx mori chromosomes are rod- and dot-shaped and lack primary constrictions.
source: B. mori chromosomes are rod- and dot-shaped and lack primary constrictions.
evidence: This is based on cited cytological observations.

claim: During anaphase, B. mori sister chromatids migrate in parallel.
source: Also, during anaphase, sister chromatids migrate in parallel.
evidence: This is based on cited cytological observations.

claim: Chromosomal fragments induced by X-ray irradiation in B. mori behave normally through a number of cell generations.
source: Furthermore, chromosomal fragments induced by X-ray irradiation behave normally through a number of cell generations (Murakami and Imai, 1974).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claim: Immuno-fluorescence studies showed the localization of B. mori chromosomal passenger complex protein INCENP along the whole length of mitotic chromosome.
source: More recently, immuno-fluorescence studies showed the localization of B. mori chromosomal passenger complex protein INCENP along the whole length of mitotic chromosome (Mon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: Electron microscopy in Origya thyellina and Origya antiqua chromosomes report spindle microtubule attachments to large kinetochore plates, covering more than 70% of the entire surface of the chromosomes.
source: Electron microscopy (EM) in Origya thyellina and Origya antiqua chromosomes report spindle microtubule attachments to large kinetochore plates, covering more than 70% of the entire surface of the chromosomes (Wolf, 1994; Wolf et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on cited EM studies.

claim: The presence of holocentric chromosomes is consistent with experimental data reporting high resistance to radiation in multiple lepidopteran species.
source: Finally, the presence of holocentric chromosomes is also consistent with experimental data reporting high resistance to radiation in multiple lepidopteran species (LaChance and Graham, 1984; Koval, 1996; Marec et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental studies.

claim: Sufficient proof exists to conclude that all Lepidoptera have holokinetic chromosomes.
source: Taken together the cytogenetic results on Lepidoptera, Bauer proposed that 'sufficient proof exists to conclude that all Lepidoptera have holokinetic chromosomes' (Bauer, 1967).
evidence: This is a conclusion from cited literature.

claim: Chromosomes of multiple hemipteran species lack primary constrictions.
source: Chromosomes of multiple hemipteran species belonging to the hemipteran suborder Heteroptera (Oncopeltus fasciatus [Wolfe and John, 1965], Euschistus servus, Euschistus tristigmus, and Sotubea pugnax [Hughes-Schrader and Schrader, 1961]), as well as from the suborder Sternorrchyncha (aphids [Sun and Robinson, 1965; Mandrioli et al., 2011]) lack primary constrictions.
evidence: This is based on cited cytological observations.

claim: EM studies in O. fasciatus and Rhodnius prolixus reporting kinetochore occupancy covering 75% and 100% of mitotic chromosomes respectively, support the presence of holocentric chromosomes in Heteroptera.
source: EM studies in O. fasciatus (Comings and Okada, 1972) and Rhodnius prolixus (Buck, 1967) reporting kinetochore occupancy covering 75% and 100% of mitotic chromosomes respectively, further support the presence of holocentric chromosomes in Heteroptera.
evidence: This is based on cited EM studies.

claim: Experimental support for holocentricity in Hemiptera was obtained using chromosomal fragmentation studies, which demonstrated that fragments induced by X-rays are able to propagate themselves mitotically through many cell generations.
source: Experimental support for holocentricity was also obtained using chromosomal fragmentation studies, which demonstrated that fragments induced by X-rays are able to propagate themselves mitotically through many cell generations (Hughes-Schrader and Schrader, 1961; Khuda-Bukhsh and Datta, 1981; Kuznetsova and Sapunov, 1985).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental studies.

claim: The presence of holocentric chromosomes in Phthiraptera was reported based on cytological observations, including the lack of primary constrictions and parallel sister chromatid migration during anaphase.
source: Chromosome structure has been investigated by cytological analysis in Haematopinus suis and Menacanthus stramineus (Tombesi and Papeschi, 1993) and in Bovicola limbata and Bovicola caprae (Tombesi et al., 1999). The presence of holocentric chromosomes was reported based on the cytological observations, including the lack of primary constrictions and parallel sister chromatid migration during anaphase.
evidence: This is based on cited cytological studies.
